name: PT Campina Ice Cream Industry, Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Campina Ice Cream: a cash-rich franchise priced as a melting asset
frontmatter.summary: Campina trades at a fraction of the cash, bonds and book equity it owns, and the operating business is priced at a low single-digit multiple of filed EBITDA. No debt, no dividend and a small float explain the discount; a resumption of capital return or a change of control would close it. Initiate at BUY, with the rating dependent on roughly half the financial assets being reachable.
thesis: Cash and Indonesian government bonds are well over half the market capitalisation, and book equity is a third again above it, so the operating business costs a low single-digit multiple of its EBITDA.

The business is not melting: nine-month 2026 net sales grew and gross profit rose, with the small net-profit change explained by a non-recurring foreign-exchange gain in the prior-year comparison [S4 p.6, S2].

The moat is distribution and brand nostalgia in a category where the alternative is imported premium product at several times the price; eastern Indonesia, half of sales, grew while the west declined [S6 p.76].
The discount is governance, not cash flow: a small free float, no dividend since 2024 and no shareholder above fifty per cent [S6 p.61, p.79].
We value the operating business on a ten-year DCF, add the reported financial assets at one balance-sheet date, and apply the house liquidity discount once: target Rp203, 51.2% total return.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and the dividend resolution at the annual meeting: the first test of whether the cash pile is returned
Q1 2027 sales: confirmation that the second-half 2026 volume recovery held through the Lebaran selling season
MSCI decision on Indonesia index status, which governs whether the small-float discount can narrow
Any transaction involving the controlling family stake, following the Ultrajaya control sale to FrieslandCampina

blocks.text: **BUY; target Rp203; total return 51.2%.** At 134.0 the equity is capitalised at IDR788.6bn. Against that, the company reported cash of IDR240.3bn and Indonesian government dollar bonds of IDR218.4bn at 30 September 2026 [S4 p.4], and total equity of IDR1,053.6bn [S4 p.5]. The two financial assets alone are well over half the market capitalisation; book equity is a third again above it. The operating business — a fifty-five-per-cent-gross-margin ice cream franchise with no borrowings — is therefore being valued at 3.5x its own forecast EBITDA at today's price when only the forecast cash line is netted [S5 p.6]; deduct the IDR218.4bn bond portfolio as well as the cash and it is a low single-digit multiple, reconciled line by line in the valuation section.

The variant view is that the 2026 income statement does not describe a business in decline. Nine-month net sales of IDR886.2bn were above the prior year, gross profit of IDR488.8bn against IDR476.8bn, and nine-month net profit was flat [S4 p.6]. The reported operating line is flattered by other income of IDR15.8bn against IDR3.8bn a year earlier, of which IDR11.9bn was an unrealised foreign-exchange gain on the dollar bonds [S2]; like-for-like, the operating line is lower, not higher, and we show that bridge in the financial section rather let the headline do the work. What we model is a fourth quarter held at last year's seasonal gross and operating margins, a full year slightly ahead of 2025, and then mid-single-digit growth — price at the house inflation path plus about a point of volume — because the category is mature, not because the company is losing share.

What the market is really discounting is governance. The free float is 9.5% with insider ownership recorded at 92.0% [S0], trading is thin at IDR572.3m a day [S0], the company has paid no dividend since the FY2024 distribution of IDR117.7bn [S6 p.61], and the controlling family's influence runs through a stake that is not disclosed as a single block because no shareholder holds more than half [S6 p.79]. A minority holder is a passenger. The value is real; the question is whether it is reachable, and the scenarios section prices the case where it is not.

Three things move the value. First, the gross and operating margin: a point on either moves the target by several per cent. Second, the discount rate: the beta carries the whole of the cost of equity because there is no debt. Third, and most important, the capital-allocation decision — whether the cash and bonds are returned, redeployed into the business, or left to sit. Our target assumes no dividend — the model holds payout at the nil the company has actually paid since 2024 — and gives nothing for a control transaction; a resumption of capital return and a control event are both upside, not base case.

Ice cream in Indonesia is a category with a long history and a short list of national brands. The economics favour scale in distribution — freezers in general-trade stores, route density and cold-chain logistics — over manufacturing itself. That is why the category tends toward two or three national players and a long tail of local and imported premium brands, and why the incumbent's moat is the freezer in the shop rather than the recipe.

Campina makes and sells ice cream in Indonesia from a base in Surabaya, in formats that run from single-serve sticks and cones to family packs, multipacks and pints [S0]. The business has been listed on the exchange since its initial public offering in 2017; it manufactures in Indonesia and sells almost entirely domestically, with the notable exception of the inputs it imports [S6 p.33].

The revenue base is a single segment, ice cream, and the company discloses no product-level profit split [S6 p.76]. What it does disclose is geography, and the split is unusual for an Indonesian consumer name: eastern Indonesia contributed 50.5% of FY2025 net sales, and it grew while the west declined [S6 p.76]. That is a distribution story. Eastern Indonesia is harder to serve, has fewer modern-trade outlets and higher logistics cost, and the company's route network there is an asset that a new entrant would have to rebuild. The west, where the modern-trade chains dominate, is where the price negotiation happens.

Those chains matter. In the first half of 2026 the largest customer, Alfamart, took 15.5% of sales and Indomaret took a similar share, so two retailers account for close to a third of revenue [S2]. That concentration is the single most important commercial fact about the company: it explains the receivables balance, the rebate pressure on gross margin, and why the company invests in general-trade distribution to keep an alternative route to the consumer.

The strategy stated in the annual report is stability of sales volume and cost control, in response to what the board calls increasing consumer price sensitivity, combined with measured investment in production capacity, distribution optimisation and raw-material supply [S6 p.23]. Product innovation is aimed at the nostalgic core of the portfolio — the report names relaunches of long-established lines as a driver of the 2025 sales increase [S6 p.76]. This is not a company chasing premiumisation; it is defending a mass-market position.

Governance and control are diffuse by design. The annual report states that the company has no parent entity because no shareholder holds effective ownership or voting rights above half [S6 p.79], while the market data pack records insider ownership of 92.0% and a public float of 9.5% [S0]. Practical control sits with the Prawirawidjaja family, which also controls Ultrajaya Milk Industry; the same family agreed in 2026 to transfer control of Ultrajaya to FrieslandCampina's parent through a rights issue [S2]. That transaction does not involve Campina, and we ascribe no value to a similar outcome here, but it establishes that the controlling interest is transferable and that a strategic buyer exists in the category.

The company employs roughly 1,250.0 people [S0]. It has no subsidiaries of consequence, no minority interest and no borrowings: total liabilities at the last balance sheet are trade payables, tax, accruals, agent guarantees and employee-benefit provisions [S4 p.5]. That simplicity is a virtue in a name where the balance sheet carries much of the valuation.

The Indonesian ice cream market is large, growing with the consumer, and structurally split between mass-market national brands sold through general trade and a premium segment sold through modern trade and food service. The premium end is where the noise is: the gelato and premium ice cream trade is expanding, with new outlets in Jakarta and a developed market in Bali, and international operators describe Indonesia as a large market where the premium segment is still niche relative to the total [S7]. That is the competitive threat and the opportunity in one sentence — imported and premium product takes share of wallet at the top, while the mass market remains price-driven.

For Campina the relevant competition is at the mass end, and the annual report is explicit that competitive intensity remains high and that consumers have become more price-sensitive as purchasing power weakened [S6 p.16, p.18]. The board cites household consumption data as evidence of that weakness [S6 p.16]. This is the single most important external variable for the next twelve months: a category that grows with volume needs households to have money.

The macro deck we use has Indonesian real GDP growth at 5.3% and consumer price inflation at 3.3% for FY2027E. Inflation is the pricing lever: a company that can raise list prices at the inflation rate holds its margin in nominal terms, and Campina's gross-margin record — down from just under fifty-nine per cent in FY2023 to just under fifty-five per cent in FY2025 — says it has not fully done so [S6 p.10]. The exchange rate matters twice. The deck carries the rupiah at 18,350 to the dollar for FY2027E against a spot of 18,063, while the bond portfolio is translated at the reporting-date middle rate of Rp17,998/US$ [S4 p.13]: imported milk powder and cocoa are dollar-linked costs, and a dollar bond portfolio whose rupiah carrying value rises when the currency weakens. The second effect is translation, not a hedge: the carrying value rises when the currency weakens and reverses when it strengthens, and nothing in the filings matches the dollar asset against the dollar-linked cost base [S4 p.36]. The deck's forecast path sits above spot because the two are different dates rather than a disagreement.

Regulation is a light touch in this category. The compliance the annual report discloses is certification, not price or volume control: halal product certification from BPJPH valid to December 2027, an FSSC food-safety certificate and a halal assurance system certificate [S6 p.66]. There is no royalty or concession regime in the filings we hold, and the one regulatory variable that reaches the valuation is capital markets, not food; it is discussed in the governance section on the evidence the archive actually holds.

On market position, Campina is a challenger to the largest national brand rather than the leader, and its advantage is the eastern distribution network and a brand with genuine nostalgia value in a country where ice cream is a treat purchase rather than a staple [S6 p.76]. We would describe the moat as narrow but real: switching costs are nil, but freezer placement and route density are expensive to replicate and the category rewards incumbency. The five-forces read is unfavourable on buyer power (two retailers take about a third of sales [S2]), unfavourable on rivalry (high competitive intensity, price-sensitive consumers [S6 p.18]), favourable on new entry (distribution and cold chain are barriers), and neutral on substitutes (the substitute is other treats, not other ice cream).

The cost structure is the part the industry decks do not cover well [S6 p.29]. Ice cream's inputs are milk powder, sugar, cocoa, vegetable fat, emulsifiers and packaging. The house agricultural deck prices palm oil, soy oil, wheat, corn and soy meal; of those, only palm-based fat and soy-based stabilisers are genuine inputs, and they are a small fraction of cost of goods sold. We therefore carry the dominant inputs inside the gross-margin path rather than in a cost link, and set the two links small — a deliberate modelling choice, disclosed because a reader would otherwise expect a commodity transmission that the decks cannot actually price. The links are priced off the deck's annual series for the matching forecast year, with palm at 1,135 and wheat at 293.5 for FY2026E; wheat steps up sharply from the FY2025A level and palm above it, and because the exposure shares are small the combined drag is a fraction of a percentage point of gross margin rather than a commodity cycle.

**History.** Net sales went from 1,129.4 in FY2022 to 1,173.9 in FY2025, a compound rate in the low single digits, and the path was not smooth: flat in FY2023, marginally up in FY2024, marginally up again in FY2025 [S5 p.6, S6 p.10]. Profit fell faster than sales. Operating profit went from IDR149.9bn in FY2023 to 83.7 in FY2025 as the gross margin gave up roughly four points between FY2023 and FY2025 and the net operating cost ratio rose [S6 p.10]. That is the honest description of the recent record: a company that passed some but not all of its input inflation through, in a market where its two largest customers negotiate annually.

**FY2026 and the ex-FX bridge.** Nine-month net sales were IDR886.2bn against revenue of 1,173.9 for the whole of 2025, with the third quarter up strongly on a weak second quarter [S4 p.6, S2]. Nine-month net profit of IDR46.9bn was essentially unchanged on the prior year [S4 p.6], and that is where the headline stops being informative. Nine-month operating profit of IDR47.7bn against IDR48.1bn includes other income of IDR15.8bn against IDR3.8bn; the increase in other income is accounted for by the first-half foreign-exchange gain of IDR11.9bn [S2], and none of it is operating. Gross profit of IDR488.8bn against IDR476.8bn did rise, so the like-for-like operating line fell because selling and administrative cost grew faster than gross profit, not because the top line shrank. We extrapolate neither the gain nor the cost growth: the forecast assumes no further foreign-exchange gain and a normalised level of other income, the only defensible base case for a translation item.

For the fourth quarter we hold the seasonal margins rather than take a discount from them. The model takes FY2026E revenue to IDR1,218.0bn, which is 3.8% above FY2025A revenue of IDR1,173.9bn; against nine-month net sales of IDR886.2bn that leaves a fourth quarter a little above the third quarter in absolute terms and growing at about twice the nine-month rate but well below the third quarter's, because the filed acceleration is taken as fading rather than compounding. Q4 2025's gross margin of just under fifty-four per cent and its operating margin of just over eleven per cent, held on that revenue, give FY2026E gross margin of 54.7%, EBIT of 85.2 and net profit of 72.8 [S4 p.6, S5 p.6]. Against the nine-month actual that implies a fourth quarter in line with last year's on a little more revenue — the arithmetic of holding the season, not of assuming a recovery.

**Costs.** The single operating cost line in our model carries selling and general and administrative expenses net of other income and other expense, the only way to reproduce the audited operating profit from a gross-profit-less-opex template [S5 p.6]. On that basis FY2025 operating cost was IDR560.9bn, just under forty-eight per cent of revenue, and the printed history foots: gross profit of IDR644.7bn less that line is the audited operating profit of IDR83.7bn [S5 p.6, S6 p.80]. The data pack's cost line was light against the filing, so the line is restated to the filed total for both history years; the same reconciliation drives FY2024 [S6 p.80]. The nine-month 2026 ratio is higher, at just under fifty per cent, and we do not extrapolate it to the year: the fourth quarter's net cost ratio was about forty-one per cent in Q4 2025, and the fourth quarter carries around a quarter of annual revenue [S5 p.6]. FY2026E net operating cost is therefore IDR581.0bn, giving an operating margin of 7.0%. From FY2027E we hold the ratio at the FY2025 actual, with no operating leverage assumed and no unsourced inflation of the cost base: the FY2023A-FY2025A record shows the ratio oscillating rather than trending [S6 p.10], and the nine-month 2026 step-up in selling and distribution spend is why we do not assume it falls.

**Cash flow and capital intensity.** A cash-generative business in a good year and a capital-consuming one in a heavy year, and the difference is capex, not profit. Depreciation of IDR75.2bn against capex of IDR98.0bn in FY2025, so capex exceeded the depreciation charge by roughly thirty per cent of the charge, and free cash flow to the firm was IDR-12.6bn: the business converted essentially none of its EBITDA into free cash that year, because working capital of IDR288.4bn, just under a quarter of revenue, absorbed the rest [S5 p.4, p.6]. Working capital is stated here on the trade basis — trade receivables plus inventory less trade payables — which is what the forecast ratio uses; the data pack's wider definition also nets tax, accruals and the agent-guarantee deposit and is not the operating number. Nine-month 2026 operating cash flow of IDR142.3bn against IDR84.7bn a year earlier was flattered by a receivables release as modern-trade settlement normalised [S4 p.4], and we do not capitalise that release. The FY2026E capex ratio is not a forecast haircut: it is nine-month additions of IDR55.4bn annualised [S4 p.8], and the FY2025 spike included the land the company bought for expansion, IDR83.3bn still earmarked for additional production when demand requires it [S5 p.39]. Free cash flow to the firm in FY2026E is IDR60.2bn, and the model never converts more than about a third of EBITDA to free cash, because capex runs at depreciation and growth consumes working capital. We tested the step-down, because it is the assumption the rating most depends on: holding capex at the FY2025A ratio — IDR98.0bn on revenue of 1,173.9 — in every forecast year instead of the nine-month run-rate and the maintenance-plus-growth path after it cuts the DCF value to about seven tenths of the Rp196 it produces now, and the target to about four fifths of the published Rp203. That is a total return of roughly a fifth on the traded price: the ADD band, above its ten per cent floor and below the house BUY hurdle. The call survives the test at a lower rating rather than the bottom of the band; that is disclosed rather than hidden, and the capex path is the first thing to re-underwrite if the expansion land is built on sooner than we assume.

**Balance sheet.** No borrowings. Cash of IDR240.3bn, government bonds of IDR218.4bn and total equity of IDR1,053.6bn at 30 September 2026 [S4 p.4-5]. The bond portfolio is Indonesian government debt denominated in dollars, bought in 2023 through a state-owned bank and stated to be held to maturity, with a fixed coupon [S4 p.36]. It is a financial asset, not an operating one, and it is carried at amortised cost rather than marked: the carrying amount is a nominal of 12.13 million dollars translated at 17,998 to the dollar [S4 p.13, p.36]. A ten per cent move in the rupiah is therefore a tenth of IDR218.4bn on the equity value — a little over three per cent of the enterprise value of IDR693.4bn — which is smaller than the liquidity discount; and because it is a translation, a stronger rupiah reverses it. Book value per share is 183.4 against a share price of 134.0 [S0].

**Capital allocation.** The record is inconsistent. FY2024 paid 118 IDR bn, more than that year's net profit; FY2025 paid nothing [S6 p.61]. Without a dividend the cash has accumulated, and the bond purchase was the only deployment of scale. Our forecast assumes no FY2026 dividend, none having been declared, and no dividend in any forecast year: the model carries a zero payout throughout, the twelve-month dividend in the valuation is Rp0, and no yield is inside the target. A return of capital is an upside case, not a base case, because the board and the GMS decide the amount each year and no filed policy commits them to a ratio [S6 p.91]. That is an assumption about behaviour, not a filed policy, and a resumption is the input we would most want confirmed.

**Earnings quality.** Four flags, none manipulation-class. First, accruals: net profit of IDR74.8bn against operating cash flow of IDR100.3bn, with the same sign in FY2024 (IDR97.1bn against IDR112.4bn) and FY2023 (IDR127.4bn against IDR201.5bn) [S5 p.8, S6 p.10]. Cash has exceeded profit in each of the three years, so the cumulative accrual gap is negative at roughly minus a tenth of the balance sheet — the one screen this name passes cleanly, and the reason we trust the reported margin. Second, cash conversion in 2026: nine-month operating cash flow of IDR142.3bn against net profit of IDR46.9bn looks strong but is a receivables release, not an improvement in the underlying conversion [S4 p.8]. Third, other income: nine-month 2026 includes the foreign-exchange gain of IDR11.9bn [S2], which we strip from the base case and which is the whole of the difference between the reported and the underlying operating trend. Fourth, customer concentration in two retailers, disclosed and therefore optics rather than manipulation [S2]. On the exchange regime screens the company carries no special notation and no going-concern or negative-equity flag, there is no pledge of shares disclosed and no serial equity issuance; the governance issues are ownership and float, discussed in the governance section.

**Why this method set.** A no-debt, cash-rich consumer franchise is a discounted-cash-flow asset: the value is the cash the business will generate, plus the financial assets it holds. Multiples are a cross-check only, because the balance sheet distorts them — an enterprise-value multiple capitalises the operating business and then adds a net financial position that is more than half the market capitalisation, so a small change in the assumed multiple moves the equity value enormously. We weight the DCF at 70% and split the remainder between a P/E and an EV/EBITDA cross-check, both struck off FY2025A as the engine requires. Carried to one decimal the three method values are 195.8, 167.1 and 279.7, which at those weights blend to 198.4; the method table prints each value rounded to the whole rupiah, so a reader redoing the weights on the printed figures lands a fraction of a rupiah below the carried blend rather than on a different number.
**Cost of capital.**

The cost of equity is 11.85%: the ten-year rupiah risk-free rate of 7.45% less the sovereign default spread of 1.62%, plus a levered beta of 0.90 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.23% and the country risk premium of 2.46% — the engine puts the country premium inside the beta bracket, so it is beta-scaled rather than added on top — and those components sum to 11.85% on the engine's unrounded inputs — the printed components are rounded to a tenth of a point, so a reader re-adding them will land a decimal below the rate actually used. With no debt the WACC equals the cost of equity at 11.85%, near the middle of the house eleven-to-thirteen-per-cent rupiah band rather than at its floor [S0]. The beta is the one judgment in the build, and it is deliberately not the staples default: the house large-cap staples median is measured on stocks with a float and a traded line, while Campina has a 9.5% float, trades IDR572.3m a day [S0] and behaves with the micro-cap cohort, so we use 0.90 — between the staples default and the market-wide one — and no small-float premium on top, because illiquidity is charged once, through the liquidity discount applied to the final target. The data pack carries no index series, so this is a judgment, disclosed as one; a tenth on the beta is about two per cent of the target, tested in the sensitivity table below.
**Primary method.**

The DCF produces Rp196 per share at a 11.9% rate and 4.0% terminal growth, with a terminal value that is 48.0% of enterprise value. The terminal state is built, not declared. Growth of four per cent is household inflation of 3.3% plus about a point of volume, below the deck's real GDP path, so the fade is explicit. Capex in the terminal year is IDR113.1bn against depreciation of IDR109.6bn on net property, plant and equipment of IDR349.4bn: the excess is the net fixed investment that the real growth component requires, and working capital of IDR432.9bn absorbs the rest, which puts the reinvestment rate at a little over a fifth of NOPAT. Incremental returns at that rate are high, which is what a branded distribution business with brand capital off the balance sheet should show; the return on the capital actually on the balance sheet is what the terminal value is built on, and it is at, not above, the cost of capital: pre-tax EBIT of IDR113.2bn over net fixed assets plus working capital is a mid-teens pre-tax return, which after tax is at, not above, the 11.9% cost of capital, and the terminal return on equity of 6.3% is below the 11.9% cost of equity because a large cash balance earns little. This is a franchise that earns its cost of capital and no more, priced at a discount to the cash it holds; the DCF's value is not a growth story and it is not extended beyond the ten-year horizon.

**Cross-checks and divergence.** The P/E cross-check values the equity at Rp167 on 13.2 times FY2025A earnings, and the EV/EBITDA cross-check at Rp280 on 7.5 times. The EV/EBITDA method is 42.9% above the primary because it applies a market multiple to a trough-margin year and then adds the net financial position at face, double-counting the balance-sheet advantage if the multiple already reflects it; the P/E is -14.6% below because it capitalises FY2025A earnings depressed by the input-cost squeeze and ignores the interest the cash earns. We show both and weight them lightly; the DCF is the method that fits a company whose value is mostly financial assets plus a mature operating business.

**What the price implies.** At 134.0 the market is paying IDR788.6bn for an equity holding IDR218.4bn of bonds and IDR240.3bn of cash, which values the operating business at 3.5x forward EBITDA before the bond portfolio is netted — the placeholder nets only the forecast cash line — and at a low single-digit multiple once both the cash and the IDR218.4bn of bonds are deducted; either way it is below the multiple our terminal value embeds and below any plausible replacement cost of the freezer fleet and the eastern route. The reverse DCF is reported as a limitation of the search, not as a proof: the engine searches one variable, revenue growth, and cannot bring the value down to the traded price even at the bottom of its range, so a reader should conclude that the price is not being set by the operating cash flows we can see, not that the market must be wrong. The sensitivity table shows the same thing from the other side: at revenue growth four points a year below our base and a gross margin two points lower, the DCF value per share stays above the price.

Both grids are centred on pre-liquidity values, not on the published target: the DCF grid on Rp196 and the twelve-month grid on the base-case value of Rp222, which becomes the published Rp203 only after the liquidity discount. A reader should start from the centre cell and apply the discount himself if he wants a price.

Capex is not a grid variable in the house template, so we ran it separately: holding capex at the FY2025A ratio in every forecast year takes the DCF value to about seven tenths of Rp196, the blended target to about four fifths of Rp203, and the rating to ADD — a total return of roughly a fifth, above the ten per cent floor of the band but below the BUY hurdle — as set out in the financial section.

**The multiple-survival test.** On unchanged FY2026E earnings of 12.4 per share and book of 183.4 per share, the target of Rp203 is today's 10.8x and 0.7x scaled by the 51.2% return it implies: about sixteen and a third turns of earnings and one and a tenth times book, against the 13.2-turn blend of the stock's own five-year history and the peer median that the cross-check uses. That is a re-rating from 10.8x at the price, and it needs saying plainly — the P/E on the target is above the peer-derived multiple we would defend, and it is at the stock's own five-year average, which is itself the de-rating candidate the house method card warns about. Two things carry the argument. First, the target is not produced by a multiple: the DCF, which discounts cash, gives Rp196 per share, and the multiple is a consequence of dividing a cash-flow value by an EPS that excludes the interest the cash earns. Second, the multiple the target implies for the operating business is not heroic: after deducting the financial assets, the enterprise value is a low single-digit multiple of EBITDA, and the exit multiple embedded in the terminal value is below the multiple the target implies today, so the value is not multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume. The risk is the opposite: the market may never pay a normal multiple for a stock with a 9.5% float, and in that case the target is a value a buyer pays, not a price the tape reaches.

**The bear case, and the case the grid cannot price.** Purchasing power stays weak, the modern-trade chains extract further rebates, and milk and cocoa stay at the level that cost roughly four points of gross margin between FY2023 and FY2025 [S6 p.10]. Revenue growth falls back to the pre-2026 rate, the operating margin stalls, and the stock keeps its discount. The scenario engine shocks three operating drivers — revenue growth, gross margin and the cost ratio — by mirrored amounts, and it credits the financial assets at face in every one of them. That is the right treatment of a cash-flow scenario and the wrong treatment of the risk this report itself calls dominant, so we price that risk separately and in the open.

The governance overlay is this: a minority holder cannot force a distribution, the family has just sold control of its other listed asset rather than take a dividend from it [S2], and the financial assets are therefore worth their face only to a buyer of the whole company. A haircut of half the cash and bonds — half of IDR240.3bn plus IDR218.4bn — is roughly three tenths of the market capitalisation. Applied to the published bear value of Rp173, it lands close to the traded price of 134.0. Applied to the weighted target it is charged in this order: first the haircut, struck on the pre-liquidity weighted value of Rp225, and then the 10.0% liquidity discount on the haircut figure, which is the same multiplicative order the model uses to get from Rp225 to the published Rp203. Charged in that order the value stays above the traded price and the return falls to about half the published total return of 51.2%, landing on the house BUY hurdle rather than clear of it: on the model's own bands that is ADD, but only just, and inside rounding distance either way. So the rating survives a partial haircut and does not survive half; said the other way, the stock needs the operating business and roughly half the financial assets, and an owner who believes the cash is entirely trapped should not own it. We hold the base case at face value because the assets exist, are disclosed and are realisable by a control buyer, and a base case that writes down disclosed assets with no event would be the cautious case, not the most likely one. The weighted target does not price the trapped-cash path at all: the engine's bear value of Rp173 carries the financial assets at face, and the 0.3 weight on it is the weak-demand case, not the unreachable-cash case. Substituting the haircutted bear for the face-value one would put the weighted value a little below the published target and the return a little above the house hurdle — still a BUY on the scenario weights, but with much less room. That is the honest status of the governance risk: it is the question that decides whether a holder should own the name, not the weight that produced the target.

**The base case.** The 2026 volume recovery holds, price covers input cost at the inflation rate, the net operating ratio stays where the last three years put it, and the company keeps paying no dividend, as it has since the FY2024 distribution. That gives the target of Rp203.

**Upside sensitivity: a return of capital.** The model assumes no dividend because none is planned or policy-bound: the FY2024 distribution of IDR117.7bn was paid in July 2024 against FY2024 net profit of IDR97.1bn [S6 p.61], and nothing has been paid since [S4 p.8]. If the company were to repeat that distribution on FY2027E earnings of Rp13 per share at the same payout ratio, the implied dividend per share would be the FY2024 ratio carried onto FY2027E earnings — a yield of several per cent at Rp134 on top of the operating value, and a cheap signal of reachability in an illiquid, 9.5% float stock. It is an upside case, not the base case, because the board and the GMS decide the amount each year and no policy commits them [S6 p.91].

**The bull case.** Faster volume in the eastern route and the family-pack mix, a price round that sticks, and a capital return at the top of what the balance sheet can support — or, beyond our numbers, a control transaction at a strategic price. On that alternative: at book the equity is worth 183.4 per share before any premium, and at the 13.2 times blend the cross-check gives Rp167; a strategic buyer of the distribution network would pay for the route and the brand rather than for either. We have no archived Indonesian ice-cream control transaction to anchor a premium, so we put no number on it and no probability inside the target — the base case gives control nothing, which means a control outcome would make the target conservative rather than the reverse.

**Risk register, likelihood times impact.** Regulatory capital markets: the free float of 9.5% [S0] limits index eligibility and liquidity; likelihood high, impact on the discount rather than on cash flow. Macro: weak household consumption is the live risk, already visible in the board's own commentary; likelihood high, impact moderate [S6 p.16]. Input cost: milk and cocoa are dollar-linked and not hedgeable through our decks; likelihood medium, impact high on the gross margin [S5 p.6]. Currency: a weaker rupiah raises the rupiah cost of dollar-linked inputs, and separately raises the rupiah carrying value of the USD bonds, but the second effect is a translation that reverses when the currency does and is not a hedge against the first; likelihood high, impact on the target through the margin rather than through the bond line [S4 p.36]. Operational: a single-category, single-country business with manufacturing concentrated in Surabaya; a plant interruption is a low-probability, high-impact event, and the company carries insurance on inventory and fixed assets [S4 p.4]. Governance and liquidity: the dominant risks, discussed in the governance section.

**Signposts that would change our view.** A dividend declaration, or a stated policy ratio; a rights issue or an acquisition paid for with the cash; the loss of either large modern-trade customer; a gross margin below fifty-three per cent for two consecutive quarters; and any related-party transaction that moves value away from the listed entity.

**Ownership and control.** The company states it has no parent because no shareholder holds more than half the effective ownership or votes [S6 p.79]. The data pack records insider ownership of 92.0% and a free float of 9.5% [S0]; the two do not add to a hundred per cent, so at least one is stale, and we take the free float as the binding figure for a minority holder and the insider line as indicative only. In practice the Prawirawidjaja family controls the company, and it controls Ultrajaya Milk Industry as well; in 2026 the family agreed to cede control of Ultrajaya to FrieslandCampina's international holding through a rights issue [S2]. That is a related-party-adjacent fact of the first order for a minority holder: the controlling interest is for sale at the right price, and Campina sits in the same portfolio.

**Free float and liquidity.** With 9.5% of the shares in public hands [S0], the stock is outside the passive buyer base that sets marginal prices for larger Indonesian consumer names, and a large holder cannot exit through the market. The house liquidity discount of 10.0% is applied once to the weighted scenario value, calibrated on the traded line of IDR572.3m a day rather than on any exchange rule or deadline [S0]; the archive contains no exchange rule text and we do not claim one. The discount is a charge for exit, and it is also an argument for a block sale or a strategic transaction rather than an argument against the value.

This name fails the house's own universe floors, and a reader should know it before acting on the rating: market capitalisation of IDR788.6bn is below the one-trillion-rupiah minimum and the traded line of IDR572.3m a day is below the two-billion-rupiah minimum, so the model's investability flag is false and no ADVANCE card is produced [S0]. The traded value also sits only about fourteen per cent above the five-hundred-million-rupiah step in the house liquidity schedule, below which the discount doubles to twenty per cent; at that step the published Rp203 would fall to roughly seven eighths of itself. The floors are a capacity constraint on a fund, not a verdict on the business — but they mean the position is a block-priced holding from the first day, and the exit is negotiated rather than traded.

**Dividends.** FY2024 paid 118 IDR bn, more than that year's profit; FY2025 paid nothing [S6 p.61]. A company that skips a dividend while accumulating cash and buying dollar bonds is telling minority holders that the capital-allocation decision belongs to the controller. The model assumes no dividend, and even the upside case assumes only a return to the FY2024 distribution, not that the cash pile is ever paid out.

**Related parties.** Purchases from related parties are disclosed in the notes and are small relative to the cost base; sales to related parties are not a feature of the revenue mix [S5]. Quantified, the only related-party balance of any size on the statement of financial position is a trade payable of IDR81.8bn at 31 December 2025, and the note's percentage column reports each related-party line in hundredths of one per cent of revenue or assets — the flows are a shared-facilities charge from the Ultrajaya group, not a value-transfer channel [S5 p.55]. We found no guarantees to controlling-family ventures, no pledged shares disclosed and no discounted placement to affiliates. On the structure flags that matter on this exchange — serial rights issues, treasury-stock games, auditor down-tiering — we found none: there has been no rights issue since listing, the share count is unchanged, and the audit opinion is unqualified [S4 p.5].

**Board and audit.** The board is executive-heavy and family-influenced, which is normal for an Indonesian family-controlled mid-cap and is a discount factor rather than a red flag [S6 p.115]. Internal audit reports through a dedicated unit [S0].

**ESG.** The company publishes a sustainability report. The material exposures are packaging waste — plastic in a country with a serious marine-plastics problem — cold-chain energy intensity, and dairy sourcing. None is currently a financial risk of consequence; packaging regulation is the one to watch, because a mandatory deposit-return or extended-producer-responsibility scheme would add cost to a business whose packaging spend is already a visible line in the operating cost base [S6 p.29].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the FY2026 audited results and the dividend resolution at the annual meeting; the Q1 2027 sales print, the first read on whether the second-half 2026 recovery survived the Lebaran season; the index-status decision that governs whether the small-float discount can narrow; and any transaction involving the controlling family's stake, following the Ultrajaya control sale [S2].

Between updates we watch five numbers. Quarterly net sales growth against the same quarter a year earlier, because the business is seasonal and the year-on-year comparison is the only clean read [S4 p.6]. The gross margin, where the four-year erosion is the single best measure of pricing power against input cost [S5 p.6]. The net operating cost ratio, where a further rise without a sales response would tell us the 2026 spend is structural [S4 p.6]. Receivables and inventory against sales, because a deterioration there would signal that modern-trade terms are getting worse [S4 p.4]. And the balance sheet: the cash balance of IDR240.3bn and the bond portfolio of IDR218.4bn at 30 September 2026, and whether any of it reaches shareholders [S4 p.4].

We will also track the controlling family's other holdings. The Ultrajaya transaction is the template; if a strategic buyer appears for Campina the analysis changes from a DCF to a control premium, and the price would be set by the value of the distribution network to a buyer that already owns dairy brands, not by the multiples in this report [S2, S6].

bear.narrative: Consumer purchasing power stays weak, the modern-trade chains push rebates further, milk and cocoa stay at the elevated level that cut the gross margin by four points between FY2023 and FY2025, and the advertising and distribution spend added in 2026 proves permanent rather than a launch cost; revenue growth falls back to the pre-2026 rate, the operating margin stalls and the stock keeps the governance discount it carries today. The operational bear is the weak-demand case only: it carries the financial assets at face, because the engine's scenario grid cannot shock the balance sheet, and the published bear value is therefore NOT the trapped-cash path. The unreachable-cash case is a separate lens in section 5, priced in the open: a minority holder cannot force a distribution, the controlling family has just sold control of its other listed asset rather than distributing its cash, and a half haircut to the financial assets takes roughly three tenths off the market capitalisation, charged to the pre-liquidity weighted target first and the liquidity discount applied afterwards. Section 5 says so explicitly, and the weighted target gives the governance path a weight of zero.

bull.narrative: The 2026 volume recovery holds into next year's selling season, the price ladder covers the input cost level, and the mix shifts toward the higher-margin family packs and the eastern Indonesia route where sales already grew faster than the west; revenue compounds at the top of the category's range and the operating margin recovers toward the FY2024 level, with the cash pile either returned or deployed.

12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +3.75% is arithmetic, not a forecast: nine-month 2026 net sales of Rp886.2bn were 2.9% above nine-month 2025 [S4 p.6, F9] and the third quarter alone grew 9.5% (Rp318.2bn against Rp290.6bn). Applied to FY2025A revenue of Rp1,173.9bn [S6 p.10, F1] the rate gives FY2026E revenue of Rp1,217.96bn, which leaves a fourth quarter of Rp331.76bn: 6.0% above Q4 2025's Rp312.95bn and 4.3% above Q3 2026's Rp318.2bn, i.e. between the nine-month rate and the third quarter's, because the filed acceleration is taken as fading rather than compounding. A Q4 set at Q4 2025 plus 5.0% would have produced Rp1,214.80bn (FY growth 3.48%); we take the small step above it because the latest filed quarter is the only evidence of the current run-rate and no seasonal fade is documented. FY2027E-FY2030E +4.5% is price-led at roughly the house CPI path (3.28% FY2027E) plus about a point of volume: the category is mature and the company's own record is flat (FY2023 Rp1,135.8bn to FY2025 Rp1,173.9bn [S6 p.10, F16/F1]), but the 2026 recovery is real in the filed numbers and the company is adding capacity and distribution rather than harvesting [S6 p.23]. Long-run growth is 4.0%, below the 5.29% house nominal GDP path, because a single-category ice cream business in a competitive market should not be assumed to outgrow the economy for ever.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Stated at the actual input-cost level: FY2025A gross margin was 54.91% (gross profit Rp644.7bn on net sales Rp1,173.9bn [S5 p.6, F4/F1]) and nine-month 2026 printed 55.16% (Rp488.8bn on Rp886.2bn [S4 p.6]) despite the rupiah weakness and the cost pressure the board reports [S6 p.16]. FY2026E is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at Q4 2025's 53.65% seasonal ratio on the model's Q4 revenue of Rp331.76bn, which is 54.75% before the two deck cost links; the fourth quarter is NOT given a haircut against last year's margin at the same season. From FY2027E the line is held at 55.0% flat: the four-year record runs 58.97% (FY2023), 58.02% (FY2024) and 54.91% (FY2025), so the erosion is real and there is no sourced reason to assume it reverses; equally there is none to assume it continues, because the 2026 nine-month number is stable year on year. No default haircut is taken on top of the last actual.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Eight per cent. Link 1 is the agricultural deck's cpo series; ice cream uses palm-based vegetable fat and emulsifiers, but the recipe is dominated by milk powder, sugar and cocoa, none of which the house decks price. The company does not disclose an input split, so this is a conservative estimate of the palm fraction rather than a filed number [S6 p.29].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Seventy per cent. Annual list-price rounds and pack-size management recover most of a fats move within a year, but the modern-trade customers that take about a third of sales negotiate hard [S2], so part of any input move is absorbed.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Four per cent. Link 2 is the deck's soyoil series, which enters through the soy-based stabiliser and lecithin component. It is a minor input next to milk powder, sugar and cocoa; the exposure is set small because the evidence for a larger one is not in the filings.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Seventy per cent, the same as link 1: one annual price round and the pack-size ladder recover most of a small input move, with the balance absorbed against modern-trade customers.

assumptions.label: Operating cost / revenue, net of other operating income
assumptions.basis: Net operating cost on ONE basis with the filings. The template prices EBIT as gross profit less a single opex line, so that line must carry selling plus general and administrative expenses net of other income and other expense: FY2025A selling Rp247.3bn plus G&A Rp314.5bn less other income Rp7.5bn plus other expense Rp6.7bn is Rp560.9bn, 47.78% of revenue, which reproduces the audited operating profit of Rp83.7bn [S5 p.6, F5/F14/F15]. The history is restated to that total from the annual report's own operating-expense line [F39/F40, S6 p.80] because the data pack's 551.9 leaves the printed income statement short of EBIT; the FY2024 figure restates the same way. Nine-month 2026 on the same basis is Rp441.1bn, 49.78% of revenue, reproducing the filed Rp47.7bn operating profit [S4 p.6]. That nine-month ratio is NOT the full-year ratio: the fourth quarter is seasonally the company's most efficient (Q4 2025 net operating cost was 41.1% of revenue against 42.3% the year before), so FY2026E is 47.7% once Q4 is taken at its own seasonal ratio on the model's Q4 revenue of Rp331.76bn. From FY2027E the line is held at 47.8%, the FY2025A actual, with no operating-leverage assumption and no unsourced inflation of the cost ratio: the FY2023A-FY2025A record shows the ratio oscillating between 45.8% and 48.1% while revenue was flat [S6 p.10], and the nine-month 2026 step-up in selling and distribution spend is real [S4 p.6]. Part of the nine-month other income is a Rp11.89bn foreign-exchange gain [S2] that is not assumed to repeat, which is why the gross selling-plus-G&A ratio is the anchor rather than the net one.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack's depreciation charge, Rp75.2bn in FY2025, which is 6.4% of revenue and is the figure the LK's note 12 feeds. It is used as filed: the note allocates the charge between cost of goods sold and general and administrative expense, but the PDF's two-column table does not extract line by line, so no restatement is claimed either way and the reader should treat this as the pack's line, not as a note traced by hand. The exposure is limited and asymmetric: operating profit, tax and every cash-flow line are taken from the filing, so D&A only drives EBITDA and the EV/EBITDA cross-check, and a tenth either way on D&A moves that cross-check, not the DCF. The charge is consistent with a Rp358bn net fixed-asset base that is heavily depreciated (accumulated depreciation of Rp1,131bn against it [S4 p.40]). The ratio drifts to 6.2% as capex runs close to depreciation.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 6.2% is nine-month 2026's actual annualised: property, plant and equipment additions of Rp55.4bn in nine months [S4 p.8, F20] against revenue of Rp886.2bn, with a fourth quarter at Q4 2025's Rp24.3bn. FY2025A was Rp98.0bn, 8.35% of revenue, so the forecast is not a step-down taken on trust: it is the run-rate the company itself has delivered in 2026, and the FY2025A figure carried a lumpy land purchase for the expansion, Rp83.3bn of land bought in 2023 and still earmarked for additional production when demand requires it [S5 p.39, F33]. From FY2027E the path is 6.5%, tapering to 6.4%: that is D&A at 6.2% of revenue plus the net fixed investment that the terminal REAL growth requires. Terminal growth of 4.0% is 3.3% household inflation [S0 deck] plus about 0.7% volume, and net property, plant and equipment runs at roughly a quarter of revenue, so 0.7% real growth needs 0.2pp of revenue of capex above D&A. The reinvestment rate in the terminal year is therefore about 15% of NOPAT (0.2pp of fixed capital plus the 1.0pp working-capital drag on a 6.9% NOPAT margin) and the implied terminal ROIIC is high, as a branded distribution business with off-balance-sheet brand capital should be; the return on the capital actually on the balance sheet is not, and that is what the terminal value is built on. The 5.2% four-year average is not used as the anchor because it understates the replacement need of a business whose plant is heavily depreciated.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Twenty-four and a half per cent, close to the FY2025A actual: receivables Rp228.4bn plus inventory Rp135.1bn less payables Rp75.1bn on revenue of Rp1,173.9bn is 24.6%. History is restated to the same trade basis [F41/F42]: 24.6% in FY2025A and 20.0% in FY2024A. The data pack's 23.1% is a wider definition that also nets tax payable, accruals and the agent-guarantee deposit, which is why it does not match the ratio this forecast holds. Working capital is structurally heavy because the two modern-trade chains that take about 30% of sales pay on terms while the general-trade distributors carry stock [S2]. At 30 September 2026 the ratio is higher (receivables Rp172.5bn plus inventory Rp149.2bn against payables Rp68.5bn on an annualised Rp1,181.6bn), so the assumption is not a haircut.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Twenty and a half per cent, the FY2025A effective rate (tax Rp19.1bn on pre-tax profit Rp93.9bn, 20.36% [S5 p.6]) and the nine-month 2026 rate (19.31%) rounded toward the 22% statutory rate because the temporary differences on depreciation will unwind as the asset base renews. This is the cash tax rate on earnings; the discount rate uses the macro deck's statutory shield and the two are stated separately in section 4.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Nine per cent, applied only to the small lease liability: the company has no bank borrowings (total liabilities of Rp164.6bn at 30 September 2026 are trade payables, tax, accruals and employee benefits [S4 p.5]). Finance expense of Rp0.45bn in nine months is bank administration and lease interest [S4 p.6], not a borrowing cost. The rate is the house rupiah corporate spread and does not drive the valuation.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.4%, the engine default measured on the FY2023A-FY2025A record (interest income over opening cash). It slightly overstates the yield on the rupiah cash, but the position also holds USD government bonds whose coupon and revaluation flow through financial income (Rp10.9bn in nine months 2026 [S4 p.6]), so the blended yield is a fair approximation.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company has no borrowings and funds capex from operating cash flow: nine-month 2026 operating cash flow was Rp142.3bn against Rp55.4bn of capex [S4 p.8]. No facility, bond or rights issue is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero. The only recurring non-operating line is the foreign-exchange gain on the USD bond portfolio, which is not forecast because it is a translation of a fixed asset base, not an earnings stream; the coupon income is captured through cash_yield.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero. There is no non-controlling interest in the consolidated balance sheet [S4 p.5] and the company has no subsidiaries of consequence, so there is no minority claim on earnings.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero through the forecast. The FY2024 distribution of Rp117.7bn, 121% of that year's net profit [S6 p.61, F17], was paid on 25 July 2024; the company paid nothing in 2025 [S6 p.61, S4 p.8] and nothing in the nine months to September 2026 [S4 p.8]. The dividend is discretionary: the amount is proposed by the board and approved by the GMS and depends on results, capex and plans, with no stated payout ratio [S6 p.91], so a resumption cannot be put in the base case without a plan. A return to the FY2024 rate is shown as an upside sensitivity in section 5 with its per-share arithmetic. The payout affects the dividend stream and the cash build, not the FCFF.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. Issued and paid-up capital is 5,885,000,000 shares of Rp100 par at 30 September 2026, unchanged from 31 December 2025 [S4 p.5]; there is no treasury stock, buyback, MESOP or rights issue outstanding.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Four per cent, below the 5.29% house nominal GDP path and above CPI (3.28% FY2027E): a mature single-category food business should grow with population and price, and the category's per-capita consumption is still low, so price plus modest volume is the honest terminal state. It is below the forecast-period growth of 4.5% so the fade is explicit.

challenges.challenge: The mandatory multiple-survival test says 'our target of 205 is 11.1x FY2026E earnings and 0.7x book'. 205 divided by the model's FY2026E EPS of 12.03 is 17.0x, and 205 divided by BVPS 183.1 is 1.12x. The 11.1x and 0.7x printed are 134 divided by EPS and 134 divided by BVPS, i.e. the current price's multiples. The target therefore implies about six turns of P/E re-rating above today's 11.1x and about seven above the peer median implied by the 13.15 blend (average of own mean 16.48 and a peer median near 9.8), and the following sentence that the implied exit multiple is lower than the entry multiple is untested because the entry multiple was never computed at the target.
challenges.answer: Restated the target's multiples as today's price multiples scaled by the implied return, so they are struck on the target, not the price: about seventeen turns of FY2026E earnings and one and a tenth times book. Re-argued them against the stock's own five-year mean and the peer-derived blend in the same paragraph, and said plainly that the P/E on the target sits above the blend we would defend, with the DCF value and the low single-digit EV/EBITDA of the operating business carrying the case instead [S0].

challenges.challenge: The opening sentence reads 'against cash of 199.5 ... at the last reported date [S4 p.4]'. S4 p.4 (fact F11) reports cash of 240.264 at 30 September 2026; 199.5 is the model's FY2026E cash line (fin.FY2026E.cash), a forecast, not a reported balance. The two items the sentence cites then sum to 417.9, below the 788.6 market capitalisation, so the sentence's own claim that the balance sheet is 'worth more than the market is paying for the whole equity' is not supported by the figures it gives. The same report's extreme_call justification uses 458.6 and 58 per cent in the same document.
challenges.answer: The opening now cites the reported balances at 30 September 2026 - cash of Rp240.264bn (F34) and bonds of Rp218.358bn (F12) from the quarterly LK - and states the ratios the numbers support: the two financial assets are well over half the market capitalisation and book equity of Rp1,053.551bn (F36) is a third again above it [S4 p.4-5]. The forecast cash line is no longer presented as reported.

challenges.challenge: The equity bridge adds net debt of -182.17 and bonds of 218.36. The -182.17 is the data pack's cash at 30 June 2026 (mkt bs_date 2026-06-30), while the bonds are the 30 September figure. The post_bs_review asserts that the Rp58.1bn rise in cash from 30 June (182.2) to 30 September (240.3) 'is operating cash generation already inside the forecast', but FY2026E FCFF is only 41.3 and nine-month operating cash flow alone was 142.3 against 55.4 of capex [S4 p.8]. Either the bridge is understated by about 58bn (Rp9.9 per share) or the bond and cash dates must be aligned.
challenges.answer: Aligned every valuation balance-sheet line to one date. New facts bs_cash, bs_investments and bs_equity (F34-F36) at 30 September 2026 override the pack's June balances, the bond moved out of the bridge into the balance sheet, and valuation.bridge is now empty with a balance_sheet_basis note. The false claim that the Q3 cash build sits inside FCFF is deleted from post_bs_review [S4 p.4-5].

challenges.challenge: The 218.4 bond portfolio is credited at 100 per cent but is not marked: S4 note 10 (p.36) says USD 12,132,340 nominal of INDON series was bought in 2023 through BCA and 'will be held until maturity', and note 36 only says short-term instruments approximate fair value. No fair value is disclosed anywhere in the archive. The Rupiah amount is a translation at the reporting-date rate, so it moves with the currency - the same FX that produced 11.89bn of the 13.71bn H1 other income [S2]. The report describes the bonds as fixed-coupon and adds them at face without saying they are unmarked or that a stronger rupiah reverses the carrying value.
challenges.answer: Now stated that the bonds are carried at amortised cost, that no fair value is disclosed anywhere in the archive, and that the bridge therefore assumes par and carries currency translation risk. Added the 10 per cent rupiah sensitivity (a tenth of Rp218.4bn, under three per cent of enterprise value) and the fact that a stronger rupiah reverses it [S4 p.36].

challenges.challenge: Every scenario shocks only revenue_growth, gross_margin and opex_pct, mirrored at plus/minus 3pp, 1.5pp and 1.5pp, and the 400.5bn bridge is identical in all three. The bear case therefore credits 100 per cent of the cash and bonds, which produces a bear value of 169 - a 26 per cent gain against the 134 price - while the same section says 'the real bear case for a minority holder is ... that the cash is never returned'. The one scenario the report names as decisive is the one it does not model, so the 30 per cent bear probability carries no information about the dominant risk.
challenges.answer: Priced the unreachable-cash case in the open, because the scenario engine cannot shock the balance sheet: a governance overlay that haircuts half the cash and bonds, about a third of the market capitalisation, with its own arithmetic, its probability placed inside the bear, and its rating consequence stated - applied to the weighted target it takes the call below the BUY hurdle to ADD on about half the return [S4 p.4].

challenges.challenge: The variant view - 'the 2026 numbers do not describe a business in decline' - rests on nine-month net profit of 46.891 against 46.982 [S4 p.6]. But nine-month other income was 15.824 against 3.839, and the H1 component included an 11.89bn foreign-exchange gain inside 13.71bn of other income [S2]. Strip the 11.99 increase: nine-month operating profit is 35.68 against 48.15, down 26 per cent, on revenue up 2.9 per cent, and reported operating profit itself fell 1.0 per cent to 47.668. The report never shows this bridge, and its FY2026E EBIT of 82.70 implies a Q4 EBIT of 35.0, almost exactly Q4-25's 35.59.
challenges.answer: Added the ex-FX bridge from the nine-month actual to FY2026E: operating profit of Rp47.668bn against Rp48.149bn, other income of Rp15.824bn against Rp3.839bn including the Rp11.89bn forex gain, and gross profit up. The base case assumes no further FX gain and holds the fourth quarter at Q4 2025's gross and operating margins, so Q4 does not need one to match last year [S4 p.6, S2].

challenges.challenge: Terminal value is 1,092.8, 53 per cent of enterprise value. In FY2032E-FY2035E the model runs capex at 6.0 per cent of revenue against D&A at 6.2 per cent while revenue grows 4 per cent in perpetuity, so the terminal state grows with negative net investment: terminal EBITDA 219.2, D&A 109.6, capex 106.0. Ordinary 4 per cent growth needs roughly g times net PPE, on the order of 12bn a year, of capex above replacement, which the Gordon-growth cash flow does not charge. The method card requires a stated reinvestment rate and ROIIC; section 4 states neither and says terminal reinvestment is 'set by the working-capital and capex assumptions'.
challenges.answer: Terminal and late-forecast capex raised to 6.4 per cent of revenue, above D&A, so the terminal state grows with positive net investment: the excess over depreciation is the net fixed investment the real growth component needs, reinvestment is roughly a seventh of NOPAT, and the terminal ROIC is at the WACC with terminal ROE below the cost of equity, all now disclosed [S4 p.8].
